djb_false_proofs:
It is true soundness bugs have been found, and the Lean community spends effort on it. But this page doesn't convey the gap between one incorrect verification and successfully misleading mathematicians about what is true: there are multiple checkers and you need bugs in all of them, without the input looking implausible on informal review.
(For example, a DeepMind researcher created a 'proof' that passed Lean and (a then-week-old version of) nanoda by exploiting a different bug in each. But if you fed that into a regular old LLM (or to a human expert, but I mention LLMs b/c they can be assigned to review even very large volumes of Lean code) it would immediately say "no, this isn't real math.")
The increase in soundness bugs found this year is notable, because LLMs are good at finding ways to their assigned goals, and they found some funny ones. And, besides fixes for the

The call for further high-assurance work is good, but let's not miss the forest for the trees: some of these have been around for decades, and all the soundness bugs they've ever had fit in a tweet! (Or close to it.)
Comfortably more than good enough for 99.9% of software, especially considering you'd still need to exploit such a soundness bug in a way that hides a further issue in the program being verified.
Pardon my ignorance but why are these proof checkers so large? Can't they be bootstrapped from a very small set of rules, which are easy to check?

There's a deeper problem — I'm assuming it doesn't apply in the case of the math proofs because the problem itself has already been formulated in symbolic terms, by humans — but I've had this problem where, an agent proved the correctness of an implementation (within reason), but it proved it against its own incorrect understanding of what needed to be done. So in one case, what it built ended up being the exact opposite of what needed to be done!
I found it amusing in that case l, that even if it had supplied me with a formal proof of correctness, the proof would also have passed, and the implementation would still have been completely useless! Because the LLM's understanding of what it was supposed to be doing in the first place was wrong.
Communication is hard!

That shows the importance of very simple proof checkers, like HOL Light.
Cross verifying proof checkers with different implementations, different algorithms is also important.

disclog_algo:
Since it's what everyone is going to be worrying about: This result does not matter practically for cybersecurity.
The best practical algorithm for solving elliptic curve DLP is BSGS (Baby Step, Giant Step) which grows as 2^{b/2+o(b)} in the key length.
This result claims 2^O(b/(log log b)) which is technically subexponential, but since that `log log b` term grows so slowly it pretty much would only beat BSGS for absolutely gigantic keys.

A randomized subexponential-time algorithm for the discrete logarithm problem has been known for close to 50 years: https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~cs812-1/adleman.pdf
The present deterministic algorithm is highly unlikely to have practical consequences for cryptographic protocols in use.

Should OpenSSH implement a config option that requires two different types of keys? If we don't know whether RSA or Ed25519 is weakened, then better to have both?
The situation on e.g. GitHub is sort of the opposite: if you use both RSA and Ed25519, then it's as strong as the weakest of the two.

Reminder: Algorithms for integer factorization essentially always have an analogue for prime-field DLP.  Usually it takes a bit longer than this for the details to be ironed out, but the surprise would have been if this algorithm didn't exist.
What does the future look like if P=NP? Are there alternatives in cryptography that would allow us to encrypt data?

harddrives: Author assumes price cartels, but this can be completely explained by supply and demand.  Hyperscalars are buying all the storage they can get their hands on; that's it.  Manufacturers are loath to ramp up supply (high CapEx), because they'll be underwater if the AI demand evaporates.

Memory, both chips and HDs, eventually collapses in price; that’s been the cycle for decades. The boom-and-bust cycle is what has driven the number of manufacturers down. My suspicion is that, in a few years, the price per gig will collapse again. AI is memory-hungry, and PC manufacturers will be pushing self-hosted AI models, which will require lots of memory. I bet we’ll see an increase in density per unit, which will bring down the price per gig. I give it five years at most. At that time, we will be seeing PC's capable of hosting a full AI model for the equivalen of less that $1000 today. It's how tech has worked for decades. There's no reason to think things have changed.
